previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for evaluation of a new, persistent right frontal-parietal headache that did not respond to usual pain medications and was associated with nystagmus. Given her history of CNS lymphoma, imaging and further workup were warranted. MRI of the head showed a stable left parietal lesion with no new masses or enhancement, but increased mucosal thickening in the right frontal sinus. A lumbar puncture was performed to rule out CNS lymphoma recurrence; initial and culture results showed no white blood cells, microorganisms, or growth, supporting absence of infection or malignant cells. The headache was attributed to sinusitis, and she was started on levofloxacin. She remained neurologically stable, tolerated the procedure well, and was discharged home with outpatient follow-up arranged. Her chronic conditions, including common variable immunodeficiency, diabetes, asthma, and hypothyroidism, were managed without change.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I understand you’ve been having worsening right-sided headaches and eye pain. Can you tell me more about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started a few weeks ago. At first, I just had nystagmus when looking far to the right, but no pain. Now, when I look that way, my right eye and forehead hurt constantly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And any changes in vision, numbness, or weakness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vision loss, but I’ve been using my reading glasses more. I have some numbness in my left leg, but that’s been stable since my back surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Given your history of lymphoma, we ordered an MRI urgently. It showed a new mass in your right nasopharynx and worsening sinus disease. We’re concerned it could be a recurrence.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. But I’ve been in remission for years. Could it be something else?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might be infection or inflammation, but we can’t rule out lymphoma. ENT will do a biopsy tomorrow to find out. We’ll also check your bone marrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds scary. Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be under general anesthesia, so you won’t feel anything. It’s important we get tissue to know what we’re dealing with.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you. What about my other conditions—diabetes, immune deficiency?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re managing those too. Your IVIG dose was given today. For diabetes, we’re using insulin instead of your pills while you’re here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my pain meds—methadone, Dilaudid—are they okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve continued all your chronic meds. We’ll keep you comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You had the biopsy this morning. The ENT team found purulent material and took tissue samples.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How did it go? Did they see the mass?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, there’s a mass in the right nasopharynx. They drained some infected fluid. Cultures are growing bacteria, so we’re starting antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bacteria? So it might not be cancer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be both. The mass is concerning for lymphoma, but there’s also a serious sinus infection. We’ll know more when the biopsy results come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What antibiotics are you giving me?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Vancomycin and Levaquin. The culture grew Streptococcus pneumoniae and MRSA—resistant staph—so we need strong coverage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to penicillin and sulfa. Is this safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, vancomycin and Levaquin are safe for you. We checked your allergies carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The tissue culture confirmed Streptococcus and MRSA. Sensitivities show vancomycin will work well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the infection is real. But what about the mass?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re still waiting on the pathology. It may take a few days. We also did a CT of your torso to check for other lymph nodes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my bone marrow biopsy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s scheduled for day after tomorrow. It helps us see if there’s any lymphoma involvement there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an MRI of your orbits today to check if the mass is affecting your eye nerves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it? I’m worried about my vision.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—the optic nerves and eye muscles look normal. No sign of tumor spread there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. My headache is a bit better since the antibiotics started.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s encouraging. The infection is likely contributing to your pain. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had your bone marrow biopsy this morning. It went well, and we sent the sample for testing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any pain expected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some soreness, but it should fade. We’ll manage it with your usual pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white blood cell count was low on admission, but it’s improving with antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from the infection or my immune deficiency?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely both. Your CVID makes you prone to infections, and the current one may have worsened the pancytopenia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need more IVIG?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not now. Your IgG level was normal. We’ll continue your regular schedule.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The preliminary pathology shows CD30-positive cells. It’s not clear yet if it’s Hodgkin’s, PTLD, or something else.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So not typical lymphoma?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not the same as before. We’re sending more tests. For now, we’re treating the infection aggressively.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We stopped Levaquin—the sensitivities showed resistance. You’re now on vancomycin only, which covers the MRSA.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show your infection markers are improving. WBC is up, and you’re clinically better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My headache is much better. Do I still need IV antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll switch you to oral vancomycin for a full 14-day course. You’ll finish it at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about the mass? Will it go away?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t know yet. The infection may improve with antibiotics, but the mass needs further evaluation by oncology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a CT today to check your sinuses. There’s slight improvement in the opacification, but the nasopharyngeal mass looks unchanged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the antibiotics are helping the sinuses but not the mass?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The infection is responding, but the mass remains. We’ll need follow-up imaging and oncology input.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my back? I noticed a sore on my buttock.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked with a CT. No abscess or fluid collection. It’s a stage I pressure sore. Wound care will help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re ready to go home today. Your infection is improving, and you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about the vancomycin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take it twice daily for one more week. We’ll send it to your pharmacy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—oncology, ENT, and infectious disease. Your bone marrow results aren’t back yet, so we’ll discuss everything at your visits.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous, but I appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here for you. Keep taking your meds, rest, and call if anything changes. You’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you soon in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—my reading glasses. Should I be worried about my eyes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The MRI showed no nerve involvement. The glasses are likely just age-related. But mention it to your eye doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any other questions before discharge?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’m good. Just ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get the discharge papers ready. Rest well, and we’ll talk soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. See you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, one last thing—my ostomy bag is fine, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it looks healthy—no issues. Keep up with your routine care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. Nurse will assist you with discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Get some rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: See you soon.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted for worsening right-sided headache and eye pain, found to have a new nasopharyngeal mass on MRI, raising concern for recurrent lymphoma given her history of DLBCL. She also had severe sinusitis with purulent drainage. A biopsy was performed, revealing CD30-positive cells of uncertain origin, with cultures growing Streptococcus pneumoniae and MRSA. She was treated with intravenous vancomycin after discontinuing Levaquin due to resistance. Her symptoms improved, and repeat imaging showed slight improvement in sinus disease but a stable nasopharyngeal mass. Bone marrow biopsy was performed but results were pending at discharge. She completed a week of inpatient antibiotics and was discharged on a 14-day course of oral vancomycin with follow-up arranged in oncology, ENT, and infectious disease. Chronic conditions including CVID, diabetes, and chronic pain were managed throughout.
